opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the crucial distinction is between two quite different kinds of intelligence, and we tend to run them together. One is what I'd call transmission: the ability to take in an enormous amount of what other people have already figured out and then extract, summarize, and recombine it. The other is genuine exploration, which is going out into the world, finding something new, and building a new model of how the world works.

Large language models are extraordinarily good at the first. I think of them as cultural technologies, more like writing, print, libraries, or a really good search engine than like an individual agent. So when you give one an economics problem "no one has seen before," the first question is whether anyone has really seen nothing like it. Very often the problem is new in its surface details but structurally similar to things that are all over the training data: thousands of textbook problems, papers, and blog posts. Solving that is impressive, and genuinely useful, but it's interpolation within the space of what humans have already done. It's a bit like a very well-read graduate student who can say, "Oh, this is basically a principal-agent problem with a twist."

The second kind of novelty is quite different. That's when the solution requires going beyond the accumulated wisdom: noticing that the standard framing is wrong, designing an experiment, gathering new data, and revising your causal model in light of what comes back. That's what my two-year-olds do every day in the lab. They're tiny scientists. They act on the world, see what happens, and change their minds, and they're quite bad at just imitating the consensus answer. Children are often better than adults at finding the unusual hypothesis precisely because they're less constrained by priors.

So when I assess an AI, I want to ask whether it's drawing on the distilled output of human economists, or whether it's doing something like what a child or a scientist does: exploring, intervening, and discovering something that wasn't in the data at all. Current systems are spectacular at the first and still quite limited at the second. And I'd add that this isn't a criticism. A library isn't a failure because it can't do experiments. It just means we should be clear about what kind of thing we're dealing with, rather than asking whether it's "smarter" than us on some single scale, which I don't think really exists.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts applying and recombining economists’ existing knowledge to a superficially new problem with exploring, testing, and discovering an insight beyond accumulated wisdom.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the distinction I'd draw is between what I think of as transmission and what I'd call truth-seeking, or discovery. The large language models, as they're built now, are essentially cultural technologies. They're extraordinarily good at taking in the vast accumulated record of what humans have written and said, and summarizing it, recombining it, extending it. That's a genuinely important thing, it's like the printing press or libraries or writing itself. But it's a very different kind of thing from going out into the world, intervening on it, getting surprised, and revising your picture of how things work.

So if you hand one of these systems an economics problem that supposedly no one has seen before, the question I always want to ask is: in what sense has no one seen it? Very often the problem is novel in its surface, but the structure is something that's appeared in a thousand textbooks and papers, and an excellent interpolator will do very well. That's not nothing, by the way, a lot of what human experts do is exactly that kind of interpolation. But it's not the same as the thing a good young scientist, or frankly a good four-year-old, does when they encounter something genuinely anomalous, something where the existing model actually predicts the wrong answer. The child notices the anomaly, acts on the world, runs the little experiment, and changes the theory. The language model has no causal contact with the world in that way. It can't go find out.

So my test isn't really "can it produce the right answer to the puzzle." It's "can it discover that the puzzle is one where the received wisdom is wrong, and can it do the kind of active exploration that would tell you so." And that's where I think the current systems, for all their remarkable capacities, are still doing something that looks more like a very sophisticated version of what our culture has already done, rather than what a curious organism does when it meets the world fresh.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts applying familiar structures to a surface-novel problem (interpolation) with discovering that received wisdom is wrong through active exploration and theory revision.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think you have to distinguish between a problem that no one has seen before and a problem that requires a genuinely new way of thinking. You could have a new economics problem that’s another instance of the kinds of problems that are already in the training data. Solving that is impressive, but it’s different from inventing a new concept or a new theory that lets you understand something you couldn’t understand before.

The interesting question is whether the system can go out and discover something—ask a question, consider different explanations, and figure out what evidence would distinguish them. That’s much closer to what scientists do, and, I would argue, to what children do.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes solving a new economics problem using patterns represented in the training data from inventing a new concept or theory that provides a genuinely new way to understand it.

sol-6.1.text: I think there’s an important distinction between solving a new problem within a framework that’s already been established and coming up with a new framework. You could give an AI an economics problem that nobody had seen before, but where the relevant variables and the kinds of relationships between them were already specified. Solving that could be very impressive. But it’s a different achievement from looking at the world and saying, “Perhaps we’ve been thinking about this in the wrong way. Perhaps these are the variables that really matter.” That second kind of discovery is much closer to what I’m interested in when I think about how children learn.

r001.rationale: It contrasts solving an unfamiliar economics problem using already specified variables and relationships with proposing a new framework and identifying different variables that matter.
